kakekotoba.reading_primary: 刈り根（芦の刈った根株）
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: 仮寝（かりそめの仮眠・仮の宿り）
kakekotoba.interaction: The reed's 'cut stubble' (刈り根) sounds identical to 'brief/temporary sleeping' (仮寝), so the physical image of cut reed-stubble in Naniwa Bay simultaneously evokes a single night's transient tryst or fitful sleep — literally setting up the 'one night' (一夜) that follows.

kakekotoba.reading_secondary: 一節（ひとよ、芦の茎の節間の意）
kakekotoba.interaction: 一夜 reads as 'one night' (the single tryst) but also, via the reed image network, echoes 'ひとよ' as a single joint/segment of the reed stalk (節), reinforcing the image of the short reed-segment as a metaphor for the brief night together.

kakekotoba.reading_primary: 身を尽くして（我が身を尽くし尽くす、消耗する）
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: 澪標（みをつくし、水路標識の杭）
kakekotoba.interaction: みをつくし is the name of the channel-marker stakes standing in Naniwa Bay; the phrase simultaneously means 'to exhaust/wear out one's body (in longing)' and evokes these visible stakes in the bay, tying the speaker's self-consuming passion to the concrete Naniwa seascape established in the kami-no-ku.

bipartite.kami_theme: A physical scene at Naniwa Bay: reeds cut down to stubble, evoking a single brief night's lodging or encounter
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker wonders whether she must go on exhausting herself in unending longing for the sake of that one brief night
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku's image of the reed cut short into a single joint/segment (一夜/ひとよ) after a fleeting cutting functions as a sustained implicit simile for the brevity of the one-night encounter, while the homophony of みをつくし (channel marker / exhausting oneself) carries the Naniwa setting directly into the emotional register of the shimo-no-ku, making the transition from landscape to passion feel inevitable rather than stated.

kigo.note: Reeds (芦) at a bay, especially when cut down to stubble (かりね), are classic autumn/winter waterside imagery in waka, associated with desolate marshland scenes and the withering of vegetation; here the cut reed evokes the fragility and transience central to the poem's mood.
